name: Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)
autonymMeaning: Mvumbo comes from the trunk of the sìó tree; Kwàsíó, “having hollowed out the sìó trunk”
place: 3rd-degree chiefdom of Nziou, Kribi area (Océan, South)
overview: The Kwasio, Mvumbo (Ngoumba) and Mabi (Mabea) live in the Kribi region alongside the Batanga, Bulu, Fang and Yasa, with relatives in Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. Fishing, hunting and the cultivation of cassava, plantain and cocoyam sustain them; the Ngúmá màɓi and M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ festivals celebrate their identity.

sections.title: Identity and neighbours
items: Integrated group, of equal weight with its neighbours (Batanga, Bulu, Fang, Yasa); most also speak French.
Closely related speech varieties exist in Gabon (makina, at Bitam) and in Equatorial Guinea (bisio).
Formerly endogamous, the Kwasio today readily marry outside the group, men and women alike.

sections.title: Territory and migrations
items: They are said to have come from eastern Cameroon (tradition even mentions Togo) and have kept cordial ties with their regions of origin.

sections.title: Social organisation and power
items: Hereditary chiefdom, with a consensual tradition: chiefs and notables appoint the paramount chief.
Everyone interacts freely; young people greet their elders and the wife listens to her husband, but these rules are fading.
Designated people dig the graves, and women look after the deceased until burial; these teams tend to disappear.

sections.title: Kinship, marriage and life passages
items: Patrilineal kinship; the wife joins her husband. Age given: 18 for both.
Marriage begins with the mpúŋgu mbɛ́ (“knocking at the door”, introducing oneself).
Palm wine is offered with fish among the Mabi, and with bushmeat among the Mvumbo; the wine is reserved for patriarchs, as a sign of honour.

sections.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos
items: No ancestor worship and no sacred site; communicating with the dead is forbidden.
Birth is a gift from God and a great joy; death, a divine punishment.
Formerly, children were not allowed to see the dead; the woman does not eat tortoise, monkey or snake.

sections.title: Economy, land and crafts
items: Fishing, hunting, cultivation of cassava, plantain and cocoyam.
The land belongs to the clan; a native who clears virgin forest becomes its owner.
Crafts: braiding of straw for roofing.

sections.title: Clothing, health, beauty
items: The Mvumbo wore a loincloth of woven banana leaves and a hat; the Mabi, a cloth whose patterns represent water, the forest and shrimps.
Traditional medicine remains alive; for lack of a passable road, people often get treated by the Baka.
Courtship: the suitor proves his strength by clearing the field of his future mother-in-law; the young woman cooks a traditional dish in the boy's family.

sections.title: Music, dances and festivals
items: Rhythms: ɓìdá, ɓopjè; instruments: tam-tam, drum, struck reed, ɲàs.
Festivals: Ngúmá màɓi (“the joy of the Mabi”) in December, M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ (“the balafon of the Ngoumba”) in June.

sections.title: The names
items: Twins are called màhùwa.
The paternal grandfather's name comes first, out of respect, followed by one or more other names; it can be changed once.
Elders are addressed as mùní nkwùlɛ́, young people as míó.

lessons.title: Who are the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)? Identity, language and territory
objectives: Name the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community and explain its name
Locating your territory and its neighbours
Telling one's origin according to tradition
lessons.competence: Introduce the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within the cultural diversity of Cameroon.
lessons.situation: A pen pal from another region asks you to introduce the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?
lessons.materiel: Map of Cameroon, cultural profile of the community (“Cultures” section of Likalo).

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Present the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community (name, language, territory, neighbours, origin) and place it within Cameroon's cultural diversity.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A pen friend from another region asks you to introduce the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community to them: who are they, where do they live, where do they come from?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What do the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) call themselves and what does this name mean? — What language do they speak, and where else is it spoken? — Which peoples do they live with? — Where did they come from, according to tradition?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Integrated group, of equal weight to its neighbours (Batanga, Bulu, Fang, Yasa); most also speak French. • Related speech varieties exist in Gabon (makina, at Bitam) and in Equatorial Guinea (bisio). • Formerly endogamous, the Kwasio now readily marry outside, men and women alike. • They are said to have come from the East of Cameroon (tradition even mentions Togo) and have kept cordial ties with their regions of origin.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kwasio, Mvumbo (Ngoumba) and Mabi (Mabea) live in the Kribi region alongside the Batanga, Bulu, Fang and Yasa, with relatives in Gabon and Equatorial Guinea. Fishing, hunting and the cultivation of cassava, plantain and cocoyam sustain them; the Ngúmá màɓi and M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ festivals celebrate their identity.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: On a map of Cameroon, locate the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) community and its neighbours, then write 5 sentences to introduce it to your pen pal.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-II — Cultural practices: ways of life
lessons.title: Traditional food and drink of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)
objectives: Linking food to the living environment
lessons.competence: Identify the traditional dishes and drinks of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), describe how they are prepared and bring out their cultural significance.
lessons.situation: Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group must present a traditional dish of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi).
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile, pictures or local ingredients, display materials.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Identify the traditional foods and drinks of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), describe their preparation and bring out their cultural significance.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “Your class is preparing a food fair. Your group has to present a traditional dish of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi).” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the main dishes and drinks? — What products are they made from? Where do these products come from? — Who prepares them, and on what occasions? — What do they say about the community's living environment?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following: • Traditional dishes: ndóá (wild mango kernel sauce), màɓáŋ / ndómbàmbi, mfugú. • Drinks: palm wine (mànyɛ̀ maléndi), haa (maize wine), cocoa juice (màdìɔ́ má kòkóà). • Fishing, hunting, cassava, plantain and macabo farming.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: The Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) mainly eat ndóá, màɓáŋ / ndómbàmbi, mfugú. Traditional drinks: mànyɛ̀ maléndi, haa, màdìɔ́ má kòkóà. These dishes are linked to the group's activities and to the products of its environment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Choose a dish of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi): write its sheet (name in the language, ingredients, steps, occasion when it is served).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

steps.instruction: Among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), traditional dances (dances of the Ngúmá màɓi and M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ festivals) accompany the great moments of life: celebrations, mourning, weddings, initiations. Instruments: tam-tam, drum, struck reed, ɲàs. Festival(s): Ngúmá màɓi, M̀pfúl Mvumbɔ.

steps.instruction: Describe a Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) dance (participants, time, instruments, gestures, meaning), then perform it with your group.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover the music and dances of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), then learn to perform one.

activities.title: I identify

activities.instruction: Choose the most representative dance: participants, instruments, attire, gestures.

activities.title: I understand
activities.instruction: Explain whether it is a dance of joy, mourning, initiation or war.

activities.title: I practise
activities.instruction: With your group, act out the dance in front of the class.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-IV — Cultural practices in communities (Level I)
lessons.title: Traditional economy and access to land among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)
lessons.competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.
lessons.situation: A development project wants to help the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Describe the economic activities of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), the division of tasks between men and women and the rules of access to land.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A development project wants to help the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). First it must understand how they work and who owns the land.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the activities of men? of women? — Who owns the land and how is it accessed? — Which products are sold or exchanged? — Have these activities changed?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • Fishing, hunting, crops of cassava, plantain and cocoyam. • The land belongs to the clan; a native who clears virgin forest becomes its owner. • Crafts: straw plaiting for roofs.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Fishing, hunting, cultivation of cassava, plantain and cocoyam. The land belongs to the clan; a native who clears virgin forest becomes its owner.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Draw a two-column table (men / women) of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)'s activities, then explain how land is accessed.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

activities.title: I propose

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Beliefs, sacred places and taboos among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi)
objectives: Explain beliefs about life and death

vocabulary.langText: tortue, singe, serpent pour les femmes

lessons.competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), and their role in regulating social life.
lessons.situation: A visitor arrives among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). Which places and which rules must he absolutely respect?

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Explain the beliefs, sacred places and taboos of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi), and their role in regulating social life.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “A visitor arrives among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). Which places and which rules must they absolutely respect?” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — What are the beliefs about birth and death? — Which places are sacred, and why? — What are the main taboos, and for whom? — How were serious offences atoned for?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present, or have the students discover, the following points: • No ancestor worship or sacred site; communicating with the dead is forbidden. • Birth is a gift from God and a great joy; death, a divine punishment. • In the past, children were not to see the deceased; women do not eat tortoise, monkey or snake.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: No ancestor worship and no sacred site; communicating with the dead is forbidden. Birth is a gift from God and a great joy; death, a divine punishment.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Write a short guide to good conduct for a visitor among the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) (3 places or rules to respect, with their reason).

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Discover what the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) believe, the places they respect and the taboos they observe.

activities.title: I identify
activities.instruction: Identify two sacred places and what they recall.

activities.title: I explain
activities.instruction: Explain the usefulness of a taboo for the life of the group.

activities.title: I show respect
activities.instruction: Write the guide for the respectful visitor.

activities.title: I compare
activities.instruction: Compare with a taboo you know in your family.

student.memo: No ancestor worship and no sacred site; communicating with the dead is forbidden. Birth is a gift from God and a great joy; death, a divine punishment.

lessons.moduleTitle: Module C-V — Cultural practices in communities (Level II)
lessons.title: Greeting, introducing yourself and counting in Kwasio
lessons.anelcac: Traditional media and transmission: everyday language
objectives: Greeting according to the time of day
lessons.competence: Use the greeting and introduction formulas of the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) and count from 1 to 10, respecting customs.
lessons.situation: You are visiting a Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of kola nuts by counting.
lessons.materiel: Cultural profile (“Common expressions” and “Counting” sections), kola nuts or small objects.

teacher.intro: Expected competence: Use the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) greeting and introduction formulas and count from 1 to 10, respecting customary usage.

steps.title: Discovering the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Write the situation on the board and have it read: “You are visiting a Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi) family. Greet them, introduce yourself and take part in the sharing of the cola nuts by counting.” The students think individually.

steps.title: Working on the situation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Questions to guide the analysis: — How do you greet people depending on the time of day? — How do you introduce yourself (name, origin, place of residence)? — How do you count from 1 to 10? Is the system decimal, vigesimal…? — Why is language a tool of transmission?

steps.title: Sharing and comparing the results (5 min)
steps.instruction: Compare the groups' answers, keep the correct proposals on the board and identify what the class does not yet know.

steps.title: Mobilising resources (20 min)
steps.instruction: Present the following points, or have the students discover them: • The community's language is Kwasio. • Greeting formulae: Àsíegò or asíɛ́ = Hello (neutral greeting, at any time of day); À síegó = morning greeting (one person); À síé àgā = morning greeting (several people). • Counting from 1 to 5: Vóhò, ɓá, Nlál, Nà, Ntán. • Elders are addressed as mùní nkwùlɛ́, young people as míó.

steps.title: Consolidating what has been learned — written summary (5 min)
steps.instruction: Greeting and counting in Kwasio are the first steps towards communicating with the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.

steps.title: Assessment of learning (10 min)
steps.instruction: Role play in pairs: greet each other, introduce yourselves, ask where the other person comes from and count objects from 1 to 10.

steps.title: Remediation (5 min)
steps.instruction: Correct together; with students who are struggling, go back over a single element of the written summary, using a concrete example from their own community.

teacher.freedom: Some knowledge (rites, sacred places, initiate societies) is restricted: in class, only what the community makes public is covered, with respect and without judgement. Compare with the students' own culture.
teacher.tips: Approach recommended by the National Cultures teaching guide: active and participatory methods (“learning by doing”). If possible, invite a resource person from the community, or propose a survey of the elders.

student.intro: Learn to greet, introduce yourself and count in Kwasio.

activities.title: I greet
activities.instruction: Learn the greeting formulas for morning, midday and evening.

activities.title: I introduce myself
activities.instruction: Say your name, where you are from and where you live.

activities.title: I count
activities.instruction: Count objects from 1 to 10.

activities.title: I pass on
activities.instruction: Teach a formula to a classmate or a family member.

student.memo: Greeting and counting in Kwasio are the first steps towards communicating with the Kwasio (Mvumbo et Mabi). The polite expressions convey the respect owed to people according to the time of day and their rank.
